hook.text: A bad database design rarely feels bad on day one.

table.text: One table, every field in it, a few orders... and the first screen works.

twice.text: Ada's ordered twice, so her email's in there twice.

change.text: Then she changes it. A rushed update fixes order one-oh-one... and misses the other.

confident.text: Now the database says, with total confidence, that one person has two emails.

legal.text: And nothing in that update was illegal. Postgres did exactly what it was told.

design.text: The problem is the design. Ada's email stopped being one fact and became copies, and every program has to keep them in step... by hand, forever.

outlives.text: And you can rewrite code tomorrow... but data outlives code.

what.text: It's answering the hard questions before your software answers them for you, inconsistently.

questions.text: Which things become tables? Which facts become columns? Which rows need an identity? Which tables point to which? And which values must be present, unique, or limited?

sql.text: SQL is just how you write the answers down. It isn't the design.

library.text: [curious] Take a library. Is a book the title in the catalog... or the copy on the shelf?

copies.text: Three copies of one title each have their own barcode, and get lent out separately.

loan.text: So a loan points at a copy, not a title.

means.text: No SQL manual can tell you that. It's about what your system MEANS.

buys-in.text: And answers like that pay off later.

ask.text: Say someone asks, which customers bought a notebook?

walk.text: With customers, orders, order items and products in their own tables, it's a short walk along links the design already drew.

answer.text: One name comes back. Ada Lovelace.

sentence.text: Store each order as a sentence, Ada bought two notebooks and five pens, and that question becomes a project.

gate.text: Design also decides what gets in. Bad data starts small. A customer entered twice. A quantity of zero. An order for a customer who isn't there.

refused.text: Here, each one bounces, and Postgres names the rule it broke.

building.text: That rule lives in the schema, so it doesn't guard one app's front door. It guards the whole building.

orbiter.text: Even a type is a rule. In nineteen ninety-nine, NASA lost the Mars Climate Orbiter because one program wrote pound-force seconds and another read newton-seconds.

factor.text: The numbers were just numbers. Nothing said which.

next.text: So where does a good design start? By naming the things your data is about.
